1.meaning: A particle meaning "when" that sets up a future scenario presented as certain — not "if it might happen" but "at the time when it inevitably happens." It introduces the whole opening clause and waits for a later verse to complete the thought ("When X happens... then Y"). Here it signals the unavoidable arrival of the Last Day.
1.grammar: An indeclinable adverb of time — it has no case ending that changes, so the final long -ā is fixed. It governs the verb that follows and frames it as a real, expected future event. Think of it as "on the day when," leaving the main reply (the "then...") to come in a later verse.

2.meaning: "It is shaken/convulsed" — the earth is made to quake violently by an outside power; it does not shake itself. The doubled, echoing form (zal-zal) conveys repeated, shuddering, all-over trembling, not a single jolt.
2.grammar: A past-tense passive verb. Its active form is zalzala ("he/it shook something"), on the four-letter pattern fa'lala; the passive is formed by the pattern fu'lila, which gives the fixed vowel sequence u — i — a (zul-zi-la). All three vowels belong to the passive pattern itself: the u and i mark it as passive ("was shaken" by an unnamed doer — here Allah — keeping the focus on the earth receiving the action), and the final -a is the regular ending of a past-tense verb, not a stray or merely phonetic sound. The attached ـت is the feminine ending, agreeing with "the earth" (a feminine noun). That ـت would normally be silent (-t), but here it is given the vowel -i ("-ti") to ease pronunciation before the next word beginning with "al-".
2.root: ز-ل-ز-ل (z-l-z-l) — to shake violently, quake, convulse (a quadriliteral/reduplicated root built on ز-ل)

3.meaning: "The earth" — the ground we stand on, the whole planet, here pictured as the stage of the Resurrection.
3.grammar: A definite noun ("al-" = "the") and the doer/subject of the verb. The final -u ("arḍu") is the nominative ending: it flags this word as the subject — the thing that "is shaken." In speech the "a" of "al-" is dropped after the previous vowel, so it links smoothly as "...zulzilati l-arḍu."

4.meaning: "With its own quaking" — a noun naming the very act of earthquaking, paired with "its" to mean the full, particular convulsion that is destined for the earth: its ultimate, total quake, the one uniquely appointed to it.
4.grammar: A verbal noun (the action "quaking" treated as a thing), here used to intensify the verb — like saying "it is shaken with its quaking," stressing how complete and characteristic the shaking is. The ending on "zilzāl" is -a (accusative "zilzāla"), marking it as the absolute/cognate object that describes the manner and extent of the action. The attached ـهَا means "its," a possessive pronoun pointing back to the feminine noun "the earth."
4.root: ز-ل-ز-ل (z-l-z-l) — to shake violently, quake (same reduplicated root as the verb in word 2)

1.meaning: And the earth casts out, expels, or brings forth (what lies within it). The verb pictures the ground violently disgorging everything stored inside it — the buried dead and hidden treasures — pushing them up to the surface.
1.grammar: A past-tense verb in Form IV (af'ala). Form IV is built by prefixing a hamza (hamzat al-qaṭ', أَ-) to the root, which makes the verb causative: 'to make come out' = to bring/cast out. (In this verse the alif written at the start of the word carries the connecting hamzat al-waṣl, but the underlying Form IV marker is the hamzat al-qaṭ'.) The suffix -at (fatḥa + a silent tāʾ, tāʾ al-taʾnīth al-sākina) is the feminine 'she/it did' marker, agreeing with the earth, a feminine noun. At a pause the tāʾ takes sukūn (akhrajat); in connected speech it takes a kasra to link to the next word, so it is read akhrajati — the fatḥa before the tāʾ is pronounced in both cases, and only the tāʾ's own vowel changes. Though past in form, it describes a certain future event on the Last Day. The opening wa- is the connector 'and'.
1.root: خ-ر-ج (kh-r-j) — going out, coming forth, exiting

2.meaning: The earth, the ground — here the planet itself, personified as actively expelling its contents on the Day of Resurrection.
2.grammar: A noun with the definite article al- ('the'). The final -u ending is the nominative case, which marks it as the doer of the action — the earth is the one that 'brings forth.' (Arabic often places the verb before its subject, so this 'the earth' is the subject of the verb just before it.)

3.meaning: Its burdens, its heavy loads — everything weighty that the earth holds within: the bodies of the dead, and buried treasures of gold and silver. The word evokes things heavy and stored away, now heaved up to the surface.
3.grammar: A plural noun ('burdens,' the plural of thiql, a heavy load) with the attached possessive pronoun -hā ('its'), referring back to the earth. The noun carries a fatḥa (the -a in athqāla-) marking the accusative case, which flags it as the object of the verb — the thing being brought forth.

1.meaning: "And (he) said" / "And (he) will say" — the past-tense verb "said," prefixed with "and." Although grammatically past, here it describes a future event on the Day of Resurrection so certain that it is spoken of as already done. The verb on its own carries an implied "he"; the actual subject is named separately in the next word.
1.grammar: وَ is the connector "and," linking this scene to the quaking of verses 1-2. قَالَ is a perfect (past) verb, 3rd person masculine singular: "he said." The internal long -ā (qāla) is the past-tense pattern of this hollow verb; the final -a vowel marks it as a normal completed-action verb. Though past in form, it is used here for a guaranteed future event. The verb already contains an implied "he"; its explicit subject is the following word.

2.meaning: "The human being / mankind" — humanity as a species, the human creature. The definite article "al-" makes it generic, standing for humankind in general, the one who will be stunned and disoriented when the earth heaves.
2.grammar: الۡ is the definite article "the"; here it is generic, so "the human" means humankind as a kind, not one named person. اِنۡسَان is a singular noun. Its final -u ending (l-insānu) is the nominative case, which marks it as the doer (subject) of the verb "said" — it is mankind who utters the question.
2.root: ء-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — to be sociable / familiar; humanness

3.meaning: An interrogative particle here meaning "what?" It opens the human being's astonished question. (The same little word مَا can elsewhere mean "not," but in this context it is the question-word "what.")
3.grammar: مَا is an indeclinable question-word — it never changes its ending. It functions here as "what," beginning the direct question that "man" speaks: "What is [the matter] with it?" Being a particle, it has no case ending of its own.

4.meaning: "What is with it?" / "What is wrong with it?" — literally "to it / for it," referring to the earth (a feminine noun in Arabic). Joined with the preceding "what," it forms the cry: "What has come over the earth?" expressing shock at its sudden upheaval.
4.grammar: لَ is the preposition "to / for." هَا is an attached pronoun "it," feminine singular, referring back to الۡاَرۡض ("the earth"), which is grammatically feminine. After a preposition this pronoun is in the genitive (object-of-preposition) form. Together لَهَا literally means "to/for it," and with مَا it idiomatically asks "what is the matter with it?"

1.meaning: "On that Day" — a fixed time-pointer meaning the Day of Resurrection. It is built from yawm (day) plus idh (the moment/time when), so it literally means "the day of that moment" — i.e., the day when the earthquake and the casting-out of the earth's contents (described in the previous verses) take place. The whole verse hangs on this word: it tells us WHEN the earth will speak.

parts.en: of that moment / that time when

1.grammar: An adverb of time (it answers "when?"). The piece -idhin is a shortened form of the time-word idh ("when"), and its final -in (tanwīn / nunation) is compensatory — it stands in for a whole clause that is understood but not repeated ("the day when [all that] happened"). Yawm takes the -a (accusative) ending because it functions adverbially, setting the time-frame for the verb that follows.
1.root: ي-و-م (y-w-m) — day / a span of time

2.meaning: "It will narrate / report / tell its account." The subject is the earth (carried over from the previous verses), so it means the earth itself will give a full spoken account, testifying about every deed done on its surface. The intensive verb form conveys detailed, thorough recounting, not just a brief mention.
2.grammar: A present/future-tense verb in Form II (the doubled middle root letter, ḥad-dith, gives an intensive "recount fully, relate in detail" sense). The tu- prefix marks a third-person feminine singular subject — "she/it will" — which here is the earth (al-arḍ is feminine in Arabic). The final -u is the indicative-mood ending: it marks a plain statement of fact about the future ("it will report"), as opposed to a command or a subjunctive/jussive form.
2.root: ح-د-ث (ḥ-d-th) — to happen; to tell, recount, report news

3.meaning: "Its news / its tidings / its reports" — i.e., everything the earth has to tell. By the Prophet's own explanation, this is the earth bearing witness to every act each person did upon it. The plural conveys the full record of events, not a single item of news, and the attached "its" ties that record to the earth.
3.grammar: The direct object of the verb ("report WHAT? — its news"), which is why akhbār carries the -a (accusative) ending before the attached pronoun. Akhbār is itself a "broken" (irregular) plural of khabar (a report / piece of news), so it means reports in the plural — the whole account. The suffix -hā is a third-person feminine singular possessive pronoun "its/her," referring back to the earth (feminine), giving "its reports."
3.root: خ-ب-ر (kh-b-r) — to know / be informed; a report, news, account

1.meaning: A two-part connector meaning roughly "because — namely, that…". It opens the reason the earth speaks (from the previous ayah): it does so BECAUSE its Lord has commanded/inspired it. The bi- carries the sense of cause ("by reason of"), and anna introduces the fact that follows as solid, confirmed content.
1.grammar: Two pieces fused together. The prefix bi- is a preposition meaning "by/because of," so the whole phrase answers "why?" — it gives the cause. Attached to it is anna, an emphatic particle like "that" which asserts what comes next as certain and is followed by a noun in the accusative — which is exactly why the next word "Lord" takes an -a ending.

2.meaning: "Your Lord" — Rabb is far richer than "master": the One who creates, owns, sustains, nurtures and brings each thing to its completion, governing it step by step. The attached "your" (addressed to the Prophet, and through him every listener) makes it personal: the very Lord who cherishes you is the One commanding the earth.
2.grammar: "Lord" here ends in -a (rabba) because it is the noun (ism) governed by anna from the previous word, which puts its noun into the accusative case — so the -a is grammar-driven, not a change of meaning. The ending -ka is an attached possessive pronoun meaning "your," speaking to a single male addressee.
2.root: ر-ب-ب (r-b-b) — to nurture, sustain, and have lordship over

3.meaning: "He inspired / revealed to" — to convey something swiftly and privately into a recipient, here Allah putting into the earth the command or prompting to speak out and testify. It is a directed, intentional communication: the earth acts not on its own but because its Lord signalled it.

parts.en: to inspire / reveal / convey a directive (form IV verb stem)
the weak third root-letter (ي), surfacing as a long -ā

3.grammar: A past-tense verb meaning "he inspired." It has no suffix at all, and that very absence of any ending is what marks the doer as "he" (Allah) — the 3rd-person masculine singular past is a zero-suffix form. It is form IV (the a- shaping at the front, awḥā), the pattern that makes a verb causative/transitive: "to cause revelation to reach" someone. The final long -ā (written ٰى) is not a person or tense marker; it is simply the third root letter, the weak ي, surfacing as a vowel.
3.root: و-ح-ي (w-ḥ-y) — to reveal, inspire, convey swiftly and subtly

4.meaning: "To it" — that is, to the earth. It names the recipient of the inspiration: the earth is the one being prompted and commanded to speak.

parts.en: it / her (3rd-person feminine singular — referring to "the earth")

4.grammar: A preposition la- ("to/for") with an attached pronoun -hā ("it"). The -hā is feminine because the word it stands for, "the earth" (al-arḍ), is grammatically feminine in Arabic — so "it" here means the earth, the one being addressed and inspired.

1.meaning: On that Day — a fixed pointer to the Day of Resurrection just described (the earth quaking and giving up its dead). It singles out that one overwhelming Day as the time when everything that follows happens.
1.grammar: A compound: the noun 'day' (yawm) joined to idh ('when/then'). The final '-in' (tanwīn, the 'n' sound on -idhin) stands in for a whole dropped clause — literally 'the day of [when all that happens]', i.e. 'on the Day when...'. It sits at the front for emphasis: 'On THAT Day...'. Functions as an adverb of time fixing when the verb 'proceed' occurs.

2.meaning: They will come out and disperse — people streaming forth from the place of standing (after resurrection and reckoning) and heading off, each toward their destination. The image is of crowds issuing out and going their separate ways.

parts.en: he / it (will) — 3rd person masculine, here matching the collective noun 'mankind'

2.grammar: A present-tense verb. The 'ya-' prefix marks 'he/it' (masculine singular), agreeing grammatically with the singular collective noun al-nās ('mankind') that follows. The stem is ṣdur-, and the final '-u' is the indicative ending, marking a plain factual statement about the future: 'will proceed'. (The doubled 'yy' at the start is just the preceding word's 'n' blending into the 'y' in recitation.)
2.root: ص-د-ر (ṣ-d-r) — to go forth / return from a place; the chest as the place things issue from

3.meaning: Humankind, all people — the whole of mankind taken together as they return from the Judgement.
3.grammar: A definite noun: 'al-' is 'the', attached to nās ('people, mankind'). The final '-u' ending is nominative, marking it as the subject — the ones doing the 'proceeding'. Though plural in meaning, it is a collective noun treated as grammatically singular, which is why the verb before it carries the singular 'he/it' form.
3.root: أ-ن-س (ʾ-n-s) — the root most classical grammarians assign to nās, linked to uns (familiarity, sociability); the initial hamza is dropped in ordinary use. (A minority instead derive it from ن-و-س, n-w-s, 'to sway/move'.)

4.meaning: In scattered, separate groups — splitting apart into distinct bands rather than one mass: the happy parted from the wretched, those bound for Paradise from those bound for the Fire. Sorted and divided.
4.grammar: A plural noun used to describe the manner of proceeding. The final '-an' (tanwīn fatḥ, the 'an' sound) marks the accusative 'state/condition' (ḥāl): it answers 'in what way will they proceed?' — 'scattered, in separate groups'. Ashtāt is itself a plural (of shatt), so it stresses many divided clusters, not one crowd.
4.root: ش-ت-ت (sh-t-t) — to be scattered / dispersed; separation

5.meaning: So that they may be shown — the purpose of their being gathered and sorted: to be made to see and confront their own deeds, laid out before them.

parts.en: they are made to see / are shown — passive

5.grammar: Purpose construction: 'li-' means 'so that / in order to'. The verb is passive and causative (from arā, 'to show / cause to see'), so 'they are SHOWN / are made to see' — not merely 'they see'. The plural 'they' is carried by the '-ū' ending (here written -aw). Because 'li-' makes it a purpose clause, the verb is in the subjunctive, dropping its final 'n' — hence the bare '...raw' rather than 'yurawna'. Note the verb is now plural 'they', shifting from the collective singular used earlier to picture the individuals.
5.root: ر-ء-ي (r-ʾ-y) — to see; (causative) to show, to make someone see

6.meaning: Their deeds — everything they did in the world, good and bad alike, now presented back to them as the record they must face.
6.grammar: A noun plus an attached possessive pronoun. Aʿmāl is the plural of ʿamal ('deed, act'). The '-a' ending is accusative, marking this as the direct object — the thing being shown. The suffix '-hum' means 'their/them', so 'their deeds'. Together: the object that 'they are shown' is their own accumulated works.
6.root: ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) — to do, act, work; a deed

1.meaning: "So whoever" — opens the conditional clause. It joins this verse to what came before (the gathering for judgement) and introduces a universal condition: any single person, without exception, who meets the description that follows.
1.grammar: Two pieces fused together. The prefix fa- is a connector meaning "so/then," linking this statement to the preceding verses. The core word man is a conditional pronoun ("whoever / anyone who"); it sets up an if-then structure, so it needs two verbs after it — the condition ("does…") and its answer ("will see it"). Both of those verbs are put into the jussive mood because man governs them. man itself does not change its ending.

2.meaning: "does" — performs, works, or carries out a deed. The verb is deliberately open: it covers any action a person commits, however small.
2.grammar: Present-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ("he does"). The ya- prefix marks the "he" subject (matching "whoever"). The final letter carries a sukūn (no vowel) rather than the expected -u: this silent ending is the jussive mood, triggered because it is the condition-verb after man ("whoever"). The jussive here gives the sense "if anyone does…".

3.meaning: "the weight / measure of" — an amount equivalent in heaviness to something. It quantifies the deed: even an amount as light as what follows.
3.grammar: A noun meaning "a weight / a measure." Its final -a (fatḥa) is the accusative ending: it is the direct object of "does" (he does an amount…). At the same time it stands as the first term of a possessive pair with the next word, so it reads "the weight OF…". Being the front term of such a pair, it takes no "the" and no tanwīn.

4.meaning: "of an atom / a tiny speck" — originally the smallest ant, or a mote of dust seen floating in a sunbeam. It signals the very least conceivable quantity.
4.grammar: A feminine singular noun. The closing -in (kasra + tanwīn) is the genitive ending with no "the," giving "of an atom." It is genitive because it is the second term of the possessive pair begun by "weight" — literally "weight-of an-atom." The tanwīn (-n sound) marks it as indefinite ("an," not "the").
4.root: ذ-ر-ر (dh-r-r) — to scatter; a tiny particle

5.meaning: "good" — goodness, a good deed, anything beneficial and righteous. Here it specifies what kind of "atom's weight" is meant: an atom's weight of good.
5.grammar: A noun ("good"). Its ending -an (fatḥa + tanwīn) is accusative and indefinite. The accusative here works as a specification: it clarifies the vague "weight of an atom" by naming its type — "…an atom's weight, namely, of good." The tanwīn again shows it is indefinite.
5.root: خ-ي-ر (kh-y-r) — goodness, that which is good

6.meaning: "will see it" — he will see that very deed: it will be shown to him, made present before his eyes, and he will witness its recompense on the Day of Judgement.
6.grammar: A present-tense verb, 3rd person masculine singular ("he sees"), with an attached object pronoun -hu ("it") referring back to the good deed. The ya- prefix marks the "he" subject. This verb is the answer/result of the condition ("whoever does… [then] he will see it"), so it is in the jussive mood — the weak final letter of the root has dropped away, which is how the jussive shows on this kind of verb. The attached -hu carries a long "-ū" sound here for recitation.

1.meaning: "And whoever" — joins this verse to the previous one and opens a conditional sentence: "and as for anyone who...". It sets up a universal rule that applies to every single person without exception.
1.grammar: Two pieces joined together. The wa- prefix simply means "and", linking this verse to verse 7. "man" is a conditional word meaning "whoever"; it triggers two verbs after it — the condition ("does") and its result ("will see it") — and forces both into the clipped jussive form (see words 2 and 6). Here "man" functions as the subject doing the action.

2.meaning: "does" — to do, perform, or carry out an action or deed. The same root gives the word for "deeds" (aʿmāl), so this is specifically about the concrete actions a person performs in life.
2.grammar: A present-tense verb, "he does". The ya- prefix marks the "he" subject (here pointing back to "whoever"). Crucially the ending is a bare sukūn (no vowel) on the final -l — this is the jussive mood, demanded by the conditional "man". The clipped ending signals the "if" half of the sentence: "if anyone does...". Grammatically present-tense in form, but it carries a future/conditional sense.
2.root: ع-م-ل (ʿ-m-l) — to do, to work, to act

3.meaning: "the weight of" — a measure, weight, or amount equal to something. It introduces the smallest imaginable quantity: even an amount as slight as the next word describes.
3.grammar: A noun meaning "a weight equal to". It is the direct object of "does" (you "do" a deed of such-and-such weight), which is why the final lām carries the accusative fatḥa -a, giving mithqāla. It is also the first half of a possessive pair — "the weight OF an atom" — which links it directly to the following word.

4.meaning: "of an atom / of a tiny speck" — the word pictures a minute ant, a mote of dust seen floating in a sunbeam, or the tiniest particle imaginable. It conveys "the smallest conceivable amount".
4.grammar: A noun completing the pair "the weight OF an atom". Because it is the possessor in that pairing, it takes the genitive case. The stem ذَرَّة ends in tāʾ marbūṭa (ة), pronounced -t- once a case vowel follows; the kasratān ٍ on top supplies the genitive ending -in and marks the word indefinite, "an atom". Stem + ending = dharrat + in = dharratin.

5.meaning: "of evil" — wrongdoing, harm, or bad deeds; the opposite of the "good" (khayr) mentioned in the previous verse. It specifies what kind of atom's-weight is meant.
5.grammar: A noun, "evil", with the accusative -an ending (fatḥatān/tanwīn). The accusative here works as a specification (tamyīz) — it pins down exactly what the "atom's weight" consists of: "an atom's weight, namely of evil". The -n marks it indefinite. It deliberately mirrors "khayran" ("good") in verse 7, setting evil against good.

6.meaning: "will see it" — he will see, witness, and find that evil itself laid before him on the Day of Judgement. "It" refers back to the atom's weight of evil: nothing is too small to be brought back and shown to its doer.
6.grammar: A present-tense verb "he sees" plus an attached object pronoun "-hu" ("it"). The ya- prefix marks the "he" subject. This is the result-half of the conditional, so the verb is jussive ("he will see"); the root's final weak letter is dropped in this mood, leaving the short "yara". The suffix -hu is the object — what he will see — and points back to the atom's weight of evil. Together: "...he will see it."
